newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC haunted by weak prices, quota-busting.
newsitem.headline: OPEC haunted by weak prices, quota-busting.

text.p: OPEC ministers gathered in Vienna Monday to tackle the burning issue of the violations of their own production quotas that threaten to send world oil prices skidding lower again.

One of the oil chiefs that arrived early for the conference that opens Wednesday was the minister from Iran, Gholamreza Aqazadeh, who has called for discipline among the 11 fractious members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries.
But neither delegates nor independent analysts see much prospect of a cut of some 2 million barrels per day of excess OPEC oil, which is above the cartel's agreed limit of 25.03 million.

Low stocks, cold weather and delays to resumed Iraqi oil sales late in 1996 boosted oil prices to post-Gulf War highs of $25 per barrel. But the oil companies have replenished their stocks and prices on Monday hovered at $19.00 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Price hawks led by OPEC's second-biggest exporter, Iran, may want to make an issue out of quota compliance. But traders warn that a public showdown could scare markets and drive prices lower.
Delegates doubted if OPEC would do more than nod through a further extension of current quotas, with some pious words from its compliance committee, which meets Tuesday.
Another early arrival in Vienna was Venezuela's Erwin Arrieta, who is alleged by oil industry monitors to have abandoned any restraint.
Arrieta said "no" when reporters asked if his country, one of those that founded OPEC in 1960, would press at this meeting to scrap quotas altogether.
But he added that "we want to widen the spectrum to consider other aspects ... We want to find spaces where there will be room for all producers."
Arrieta said, "The main act in the oil sector is not OPEC."
That appeared to be a reference to a plan to restructure OPEC on regional lines in a way that would, in effect, free Venezuela to sell as much as it wanted to the United States.
OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia is cool to that idea and Western industry officials believe it is a non-starter.
The Saudis, who have a huge quota of 8.0 million barrels, with Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, form a core of big Gulf Arab sellers who support oil prices by adhering to limits.
Venezuelan state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela has called for OPEC to stop using quotas to try to defend prices and to opt instead for a strategy of increasing market share to boost revenues.
More important for short-term price direction would be any news from Iraq about when oil exports are likely to resume under the United Nations oil-for-food deal.
The U.N. officially renewed the deal allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil for another six months from June 8.
Iraqi exports averaged 660,000 barrels a day in the first six months of the deal.

OPEC states are feeling the loss of revenue but traders say prices would have to fall much further before the cartel would risk igniting a dispute between core members like Saudi Arabia, which sticks to quotas, and seasoned overproducers like Venezuela.
The cartel, founded in Baghdad in 1960 to help Third World oil producers, has lost much of its influence in recent years as most members decided to pump at full capacity.
